key: Thee (alone) we worship; Thee (alone) we ask for help.
s: Midway through the opening surah, the praise of Allah turns into direct address; al-Tabari, on 1:5, reads the worship as humbling and abasing oneself before Him alone, preferring this to hope and fear because to the Arabs servitude is rooted in lowliness.
src: al-Tabari, Jāmiʿ al-bayān, on 1:5, the Arabic text of the Tarteel QUL library via spa5k/tafsir_api, commit 9ae590a (2026)

evidence.words: لك اللهم نَخشعُ ونَذِلُّ ونستكينُ، إقرارًا لك يا رَبنا بالرُّبوبية لا لغيرك … وإنما اخترنا البيان عن تأويله بأنه بمعنى نَخشع ونذلّ ونستكينُ، دون البيان عنه بأنه بمعنى نرجو ونَخاف- وإن كان الرّجاء والخوف لا يكونان إلا مع ذلة- لأنّ العبودية، عندَ جميع العرب أصلُها الذلّة
evidence.gloss: To Thee, O God, we humble ourselves, abase ourselves and submit, acknowledging Thy lordship and no other’s … We chose to explain it as humbling, abasing and submitting rather than as hoping and fearing (though hope and fear come only with abasement) because servitude, among all the Arabs, has abasement as its root.

reason: Key verse verbatim (verse.js ok, Al-Fatiha 1:5, at 4). Plain sense faithful: 1:1 to 1:4 praise Allah in the third person and 1:5 turns to address Him, fifth of seven ayahs; no four-word run from the verse. In the packet on 1:5 al-Tabari glosses iyyaka naʿbudu as humbling, abasing and submitting to God alone, reports Ibn ʿAbbas’s wording (we affirm Thy oneness, fear and hope), and says he chose to explain it by humbling rather than by hope and fear because servitude among the Arabs is rooted in abasement, with the paved road (muʿabbad) as witness. The sentence carries his gloss, his stated preference and his reason without drift; it takes nothing from Pickthall’s parentheses. Evidence cut by script from the packet text. Entry-check ok.
